items.title: CHGIS, Version 6
items.note: Release of the time-series county and prefecture boundary data used to map prefecture-level population reconstructions for Ming and Qing benchmark years.

items.title: Climate, disasters, wars and the collapse of the Ming Dynasty
items.who: Q. Liu, G. Li, D. Kong and B. Huang
items.note: Sets late Ming temperature and precipitation series against disaster and war records to argue for compounding climatic and military pressures behind the collapse.

items.title: On the Trail of the Yellow Tiger: War, Trauma, and Social Dislocation in Southwest China during the Ming-Qing Transition
items.note: Study of Sichuan's devastation that attributes much of the loss to decades of war, banditry, famine and disease after Zhang Xianzhong's death in 1647.

items.title: China, Europe, and the Great Divergence: A Study in Historical National Accounting, 980–1850
items.who: S. Broadberry, H. Guan and D. D. Li
items.note: Historical national accounts for China whose per capita estimates rest on population series drawn partly from Cao Shuji's Ming reconstruction.

items.title: Local Gazetteers Research Tools: Overview and Research Application
items.who: S.-P. Chen, K. J. Hammond, A. Gerritsen et al.
items.note: Describes LoGaRT, the Max Planck Institute's search and tagging tool across thousands of digitized gazetteers, the main source for prefecture-level household figures.

items.title: Population Change
items.who: S. Cao, D. Yan and R. von Glahn
items.venue: The Cambridge Economic History of China, vol. 1
items.note: Synthesis of population change from 1000 to 1800, including the late Ming peak and the seventeenth-century decline.

items.title: The Little Ice Age and the Fall of the Ming Dynasty: A Review
items.note: Reviews English-language climate-collapse studies and cautions against simple models linking cold, drought and population decline uniformly across the empire.

items.title: The Price of Collapse: The Little Ice Age and the Fall of Ming China
items.note: Uses grain prices recorded in local sources to trace the subsistence crises of the 1610s and 1640s that drove late Ming mortality.

items.title: The Population History of China (1368–1953)
items.note: Prefecture-level figures for 1393, 1580, 1630, 1680 and later benchmarks, with models and databases, including a chapter on the rapid Ming-Qing decline.

items.title: The spatio-temporal evolution of the Chongzhen drought (1627–1644) in China and its impact on famine
items.who: S. Chen, Y. Su, X. Chen and L. E. Yang
items.note: Maps 1,802 drought and 1,977 famine records to reconstruct where and when the Chongzhen drought struck, the main climatic driver of 1640s mortality.

items.title: Crunching Numbers in Ming Times: What Population Censuses Can Tell about Chinese Migration towards the South
items.venue: Journal of the European Association for Chinese Studies
items.note: Compares Ming census figures across the Shilu, Mingshi, Da Ming huidian and gazetteers, finding stagnant or negative registered growth in parts of the south.
